name: Jade Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, forty-three, an electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I do normal house wiring and shop repairs, and I know when an unusual fault needs the firm's specialist rather than a guess from me. I like the little thank-you when the freezer is running again; I don't like explaining a late finish at home for the third evening in a row.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like just now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Paul drives a delivery van, and our children are ten and fourteen. We've got a mortgage, two months of expenses saved and typical pay from my job; a few other electrical firms operate nearby. The mortgage's fixed-payment period ends in two months, so the next payment figure is already worrying me. I use AI occasionally for draft customer notes, after a colleague has tested it, then check it against what I actually did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's nothing wrong with a tool that does one useful thing. I'd tell the owner to keep the good bits and stop buying things just because another firm bought them. My customers want a repair they can trust more than a story about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the mortgage change even if the work carries on much as it is. We have two months saved, not two years, and I don't yet know the new payment. A quiet AI story doesn't make the next bank letter any smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same repair shifts now and in the first year, checking occasional AI notes against my test sheet. This week Paul and I would ask the lender for the actual next-payment options and compare the total costs. We'd pause our planned new carpet until the payment is clear; the old carpet is ugly but sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the letter, not frightened of my toolbox. I can enjoy a repair going well and still find myself checking the post as soon as I get home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mortgage number would you ask for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The full monthly payment, then the fees and total interest under each option. A cheaper first month isn't necessarily the cheaper arrangement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change lenders straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after comparing written terms, charges and what we qualify for. Asking for figures is something we can do now; getting a different agreement isn't something I can assume.

say: I'd keep **useful small tools** without copying every subscription another firm has bought.
I think customers value **trustworthy repairs** more than a story about the future.
think: I'm already **anxious about the mortgage**, with its fixed-payment period ending in two months.
Our **two-month reserve** buys some room, but the new payment is still unknown.
do: Keep **repair shifts** and check occasional AI notes against actual test results.
Ask the lender this week for **written payment options**, fees and total interest costs.
Pause the **new carpet** until the mortgage payment is clear, keeping the sound existing one.
feel: **Anxious** about the bank letter, while still enjoying familiar practical work.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story doesn't make the next bank letter any smaller.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** comes from a concrete mortgage reset rather than an invented employment collapse in the mild AI picture.
She seeks **actual written terms** before assuming a refinancing option is available, while carpet spending remains an uncommitted choice.

steps.text: Keep the usual home and shop repair shifts
Pause the uncommitted carpet purchase until the new mortgage payment is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster quotes are useful if they fit the work we actually find. I'd agree to a paid test once someone has tried it on finished jobs. I'd tell the owner plainly if a tool gets a neat answer by leaving the awkward work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid hours could shrink if a cheaper quote becomes a smaller allowance for the same repair. The physical work still needs doing, so I don't expect AI to remove it all in this picture. With the mortgage payment changing, even a small cut in take-home pay would matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a three-week paid AI quoting trial after the estimator checks the tool on completed visits. I'd record actual hours and missing materials, keeping my normal weekly pay during the test. In the first year I'd compare advertised local repair posts if the owner cuts paid hours, moving only after a signed offer improves our budget after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but willing to try a system once I can see the result. I don't want to refuse a useful change, and I don't want to pay for its mistakes through my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before accepting the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Written confirmation that the trial hours are paid and my usual weekly wage stays the same. I'd also want the estimator available to check errors, rather than make a price promise I have to defend alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another repair job worth the move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guaranteed hours, the real travel cost and a wage that works with the mortgage. A higher hourly figure isn't enough if the week has fewer paid hours.

say: I'd support **tested faster quoting** when it includes the real work rather than omitting awkward tasks.
I'd tell the owner about **missing repair time** instead of quietly making the result look better.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** if cheap quotes reduce the allowance for work that still needs doing.
Even a **small pay cut** matters while the next mortgage payment remains unsettled.
do: Trial quoting for **three paid weeks** after estimator checks, retaining normal weekly pay and access to error checks.
Record **actual hours and materials** against the tool's results.
Compare **advertised repair posts** after cuts, moving only with guaranteed hours and signed wages improving the mortgage budget after travel.
feel: **Anxious but open**, wanting evidence before either refusing a tool or accepting its wage effects.
S1.quote: A higher hourly figure isn't enough if the week has fewer paid hours.
fieldNote: Her **steady adoption** waits for completed-job evidence, paid trial terms and help checking errors rather than treating novelty as proof.
The **job comparison** protects guaranteed hours and net household money, so a superficially higher rate does not become an unsupported improvement.

steps.text: Trial quoting for three paid weeks after checks, with normal weekly pay retained
Move after cuts only with signed repair offer, guaranteed hours and improved mortgage budget after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning changes in 2028 and the physical robots follow around 2031, so the gap is a chance to prepare, not a guarantee. I'd ask which paid tasks the firm expects to offer at each point. I believe in earning our way, but a family needs an offer it can actually accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big loss of my repair hours once robots handle ordinary fitting around 2031 and larger contractors win more of the work. Paul's driving could face physical automation too, though I can't tell the exact pace for his firm. Two months saved won't cover a long gap in both wages, especially if the mortgage rises first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Paul and I would write a budget for lower income from each of us and ask the lender about hardship options and total costs. We'd ask my brother about particular school pickups if one of us gets a paid interview or training place, without assuming he's free. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply to advertised service posts only with paid practical training and signed wages that cover bills after travel, keeping this job until the offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even while I can see the next calls to make. I don't want my children hearing every frightened calculation I do after they've gone to bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're checking work and money carefully and postponing the carpet, not cancelling their whole lives. I'd be honest that things might change without promising a house is safe when I haven't got the figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would service work be protected from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't promise that. I'd compare actual work that pays at the time rather than call a different job title a permanent escape.

say: I'd ask for **paid tasks** at both dates, rather than treat the gap before robots as permanent safety.
I'd want **real job offers** that a mortgage-paying family can actually afford to accept.
think: I expect **major repair-hour losses** when robots reach ordinary fitting around 2031 and larger contractors win work.
Paul's **driving income** could also face automation, while two months saved cannot cover a long household wage gap.
do: Test a **lower-income budget** and ask the lender about hardship terms and total borrowing costs.
Ask my brother about **specific school pickups** if a paid interview or training place arises.
Apply after 2028 for **posted service jobs** only with paid practical training and affordable signed wages after travel.
feel: **Alarmed**, making practical enquiries while keeping frightened late-night calculations away from the children.
S2.quote: I don't want my children hearing every frightened calculation I do after they've gone to bed.
fieldNote: Her **main expected loss** follows robots around 2031, while the nearer mortgage change limits room to prepare during the thinking-work interval.
Childcare and **lender assistance** remain conditional, and service work requires actual paid training rather than a claim to permanent automation safety.

steps.text: Ask the lender about hardship terms and total borrowing costs
Ask my brother about specific pickups if paid interviews or training arise
Apply after 2028 for service posts with paid training, affordable signed wages after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a careful person try a proven course before taking a leap. I'd favour a paid apprenticeship-style place where the employer can name the work afterwards. A certificate is useful only if I know what it lets me do on a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages could shrink, but I have longer to find a practical route before the planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so I still need paid work rather than a retirement assumption. More time would let me check what previous learners actually do for wages now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask two former learners about the next small equipment-servicing class and verify the workshop timetable with the provider. I'd enrol next year only with employer-paid fees, my full weekly pay protected and supervised practice on working equipment. In the first year after 2031 I'd seek a paid service shift weekly only if real bookings exist and total pay and hours stay unchanged; we'd save forty monthly only when essential bills allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a slower breathing space than in 2028. I'd rather ask the same question twice now than pay for a mistake the family can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the learners describe different equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to see the actual kit and the timetable before signing anything. I'd wait if I couldn't get a clear answer, rather than choose whichever story sounds more comforting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the service shift pays more per hour but replaces two ordinary shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd need the full weekly pay and hours protected before accepting. I don't want an interesting new duty to hide a cut in the mortgage money.

say: I'd favour **proven paid learning** where the employer names the real work afterwards.
I'd want a course to explain **practical competence**, rather than sell a certificate with a hopeful title.
think: Both **wages could shrink**, but five years gives us longer to check practical routes before 2031.
At **fifty-one in 2034**, I need paid work rather than assuming retirement will arrive before robots.
do: Check and enrol next year in **equipment-servicing class** only with employer-paid fees, full weekly pay and supervised practice on working equipment.
Seek **weekly service shifts** after 2031 only with real bookings and unchanged total pay and hours.
Save **forty monthly** only when essential household bills allow.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, willing to ask repeated questions before paying for a mistake.
S3.quote: I don't want an interesting new duty to hide a cut in the mortgage money.
fieldNote: Her **course checks** fit steady adoption, including a pause if earlier learners and the provider cannot explain what equipment is actually available.
Both **weekly pay and hours** must stay protected on service shifts, and the saving target remains subordinate to necessary household bills.

steps.text: Take employer-funded equipment-servicing class next year only with full weekly pay and supervised working equipment practice
Take service shifts after 2031 only with real bookings and unchanged pay and hours
Save forty monthly only when essential household bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children can explore work without being pushed into my trade because it looks safer today. I'd ask the school about free workplace visits in fields they choose. I'd still back paid adult apprenticeships, because bills don't disappear when a parent has to learn again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning doesn't settle the mortgage payment changing this year, so I'm still anxious about the household money. I'll be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be twenty and twenty-four in 2036, but I can't assume they need no help or that our mortgage is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the proven class now and use the same paid-fee, full-weekly-pay and supervised-practice conditions before enrolling. This year I'd ask the school about free work visits, and save forty monthly only if the new mortgage payment leaves room after essentials. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare actual service vacancies if hours fall, keeping my current job until an affordable written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this year's letter and less rushed about the distant change. I can give the children room to be curious without treating every interest as a financial forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the forty-saving plan wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual new mortgage payment, if it uses the spare money. I'd rather pay what we owe than borrow to pretend the saving target is working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new machinery to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before I knew the full price, maintenance costs and real paid work for it. None of those is a number I have now, so a purchase isn't in my plan.

say: I'd support **free varied work visits** rather than push the children into one supposedly safe trade.
I'd back **paid adult apprenticeships** because parents still owe ordinary bills while learning.
think: The **mortgage reset this year** keeps household money worrying despite a decade of technological warning.
I cannot assume **adult children** need no help or that our mortgage is cleared when robots arrive around 2039.
do: Enrol in **equipment-servicing class** only with employer-paid fees, full weekly pay and supervised practice on working equipment.
Ask for **free school work visits**, keeping the children's interests open.
Save forty monthly only after the **new mortgage payment** and essential bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious about present bills**, but less hurried by the long-term change and able to support the children's curiosity.
S4.quote: I'd rather pay what we owe than borrow to pretend the saving target is working.
fieldNote: Her **mortgage reset** remains a current fact across scenarios, so a decade's warning cannot itself restore near-term financial security.
She excludes **unpriced machinery** from actions and keeps future adult children's possible earnings outside the household mortgage plan.

steps.text: Take employer-funded equipment-servicing class only with full weekly pay and supervised practice on working equipment
Ask the school for free work visits across the children’s chosen fields
Save forty monthly only after the new mortgage payment and essentials

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because robots around 2031 could cut our physical-work incomes before we have much room in the budget. Paid practical training with the full weekly wage protected would help. I'd want an employer to show the actual job and hours, and the lender to explain any mortgage help in writing with its total cost.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a family is already waiting for a difficult letter before you ask about a new future. I'm not starting this conversation with an empty budget and an empty calendar. I can prepare for tomorrow more honestly when I know what next month's house payment is.

headlineQuote: I can prepare for tomorrow more honestly when I know what next month's house payment is.
portrait: Jade is a **43-year-old licensed electrician** with a vocational certificate, experienced in ordinary house wiring and shop repairs.
She has **two months saved**, typical pay, some local firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with delivery-driving partner Paul.
Her **mortgage payment resets** in two months, keeping the mild scenario anxious before any new AI disruption.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleague checks and wants proven practical learning with paid fees, weekly wages and actual work conditions protected.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring physical-work income cuts around 2031 before the household has enough financial room.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** must protect full weekly wages and show actual job tasks and hours.
Any **mortgage help** needs written terms and a clear total cost.
